course_title: Advanced Topics in Linguistics: The Romance Languages
subject: LING
course_description: Investigation of a particular issue or topic in the study of language, linguistics, and communication on an advanced level. May be repeated when topic varies.
course_notes: (Same as SPAN 485 3, PORT 485 1) This course will explore the structural and social development of the Romance languages, focusing on the "big four" named languages: French, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. The first part of the course will trace and compare the ways in which these languages developed from Latin, including changes in sounds (phonology), grammar (morphology and syntax), lexicon, and use (pragmatics). In so doing, we will consider how general phenomena of language acquisition and cognition have influenced such changes in the past and present. Students will also gain a practical ability to read all these languages. The second part of the course will explore how such structural changes were influenced by social and cultural factors (for instance, dialect diversification, language contact, ideologies). This part will also examine factors and processes that have influenced changes in the status/prestige of each variety, in Europe and beyond; these include colonialism, standardization (language academies), and nationalism. Special attention will be given to a) recent debates about gender inclusivity and its effects on structure and use, as well as to b) globalization. The final part of the course will examine changes in structure and status of varieties of Romance that have arisen in diverse (post)colonial contexts, such as the original Lingua Franca, French-based Haitian Creole, Quebec French, Portuguese-based Cabo Verdean Creole, Papiamento, Portuñol, and the Italian-influenced Spanish of Buenos Aires (exact selection will depend in part on student interests). Prerequisites: Students need some background in phonetics and linguistics, along with some prior knowledge of at least one Romance language or Latin. Courses such as Linguistics 101 and 201, as well as Span/Ling 303 and 304, serve as good foundations for this course, but others may as well. Students should have completed the equivalent of 2 years of high school study (=1 year of college study) of any Romance language or Latin. Students with questions about any of this should contact Professor Tuten at dtuten@emory.edu.
